questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which OSI layer is primarily responsible for routing packets between different networks?
questions.explanation: The network layer provides logical addressing and routing; routers forward IP packets at this layer.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which OSI layer handles framing and link-local MAC addressing?
questions.explanation: The data-link layer packages data into frames and uses link-layer addresses such as Ethernet MAC addresses.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: TCP and UDP belong to which TCP/IP layer?
questions.explanation: TCP and UDP provide process-to-process transport using port numbers above IP.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A sender adds an IP header and then an Ethernet header. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation adds protocol-specific headers as data moves down the stack.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which device regenerates a physical signal without examining MAC or IP addresses?
questions.explanation: A repeater operates at the physical layer and regenerates signals rather than making address-based forwarding decisions.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A switch receives an Ethernet frame with an unknown unicast destination. What does it normally do?
options: Flood it to other forwarding ports in the same VLAN
Send it only to the default gateway
questions.explanation: Unknown unicast traffic is flooded within the VLAN, excluding the ingress port, until the destination is learned.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which address does a switch use to learn entries in its MAC address table?
options: Source MAC address of received frames
questions.explanation: A switch associates the source MAC address with the ingress port and VLAN.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the main purpose of Spanning Tree Protocol in an Ethernet network?
questions.explanation: STP blocks redundant Layer-2 paths when necessary so broadcast frames do not circulate indefinitely.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which IEEE standard is associated with VLAN tagging?
questions.explanation: IEEE 802.1Q defines VLAN tagging; 802.1X concerns port-based access control.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Two hosts are in different VLANs. What is normally required for them to communicate?
questions.explanation: VLANs separate Layer-2 broadcast domains; communication between them requires Layer-3 routing and appropriate policy.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the length of a conventional Ethernet MAC address?
questions.explanation: An Ethernet MAC address is conventionally 48 bits, often written as six hexadecimal octets.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does full-duplex switched Ethernet eliminate on a point-to-point link?
options: The need for CSMA/CD collision handling
questions.explanation: Full duplex allows simultaneous sending and receiving on separate paths, so CSMA/CD collision detection is unnecessary.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does a VLAN primarily create?
questions.explanation: A VLAN groups ports into a separate Layer-2 broadcast domain independent of physical placement.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which IPv4 address belongs to a private range?
questions.explanation: The private ranges include 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. 172.20.4.8 lies within 172.16/12.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which address is an IPv4 loopback address?
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.0/8 is reserved for loopback; 127.0.0.1 commonly identifies the local host.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A host assigns itself 169.254.20.3 after DHCP failure. What type of address is this?
questions.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is IPv4 link-local and is not intended to be forwarded by routers.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, compared with IPv4's 32 bits.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which IPv6 mechanism replaces ARP for resolving a neighbor's link-layer address?
questions.explanation: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 neighbor solicitation and advertisement messages.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What happens to an IPv4 packet's TTL at each router that forwards it?
options: It is copied into the TCP port
questions.explanation: Each router decrements TTL; a packet reaching zero is discarded, limiting routing loops.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which route is preferred when multiple routing-table prefixes match a destination?
options: The route with the largest MTU always
The route with the shortest prefix always
The first route learned regardless of prefix
The route with the longest matching prefix
The route with the most host bits
questions.explanation: Longest-prefix matching chooses the most specific route before considering preferences among equivalent prefixes.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does PAT allow several private hosts to share?
options: One public IPv4 address using different transport ports
One identical MAC address on the same LAN
questions.explanation: Port Address Translation distinguishes sessions using transport-layer ports while reusing a public address.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A host wants to reach a destination outside its subnet. Which local MAC address does it normally resolve?
options: The DNS root server's MAC address
The broadcast MAC of every subnet
The remote server's MAC address across the Internet
questions.explanation: The host sends the frame to its next-hop gateway; the IP destination remains the remote host.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which IPv6 address represents loopback?
questions.explanation: ::1 is IPv6 loopback; :: is unspecified, ff00::/8 is multicast and fe80::/10 is link-local.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which routing protocol is a link-state interior gateway protocol?
questions.explanation: OSPF builds a link-state database and computes shortest paths within an autonomous system.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol is primarily used for routing between autonomous systems on the Internet?
questions.explanation: BGP exchanges reachability and policy information between autonomous systems.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which metric is used by classic RIP, with 16 representing infinity?
questions.explanation: RIP uses hop count and permits at most 15 usable hops; 16 means unreachable.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which algorithm is commonly associated with OSPF's shortest-path calculation?
questions.explanation: OSPF runs a shortest-path-first computation based on Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which transport protocol provides an ordered, reliable byte stream?
questions.explanation: TCP uses sequencing, acknowledgements and retransmissions to deliver a reliable ordered stream.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the correct order of the normal TCP three-way handshake?
questions.explanation: The initiator sends SYN, the peer responds with SYN-ACK, and the initiator acknowledges with ACK.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which TCP field principally advertises how much data the receiver can accept?
questions.explanation: The advertised receive window implements receiver-side flow control.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How does TCP congestion control differ from flow control?
options: It responds to network capacity rather than only receiver capacity
questions.explanation: Congestion control protects the network; flow control protects the receiver from an excessive sending rate.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which application is often best served by UDP when low delay matters more than retransmitting late data?
questions.explanation: Real-time voice can tolerate some loss but is sensitive to delay; UDP allows the application to manage this trade-off.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What identifies a TCP connection between two endpoints?
options: Source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port
questions.explanation: The four endpoint fields distinguish a TCP connection; the transport protocol is included when describing a general five-tuple flow.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the purpose of a TCP retransmission timeout?
options: Resend data not acknowledged within an estimated interval
questions.explanation: When acknowledgement does not arrive in time, TCP retransmits; its timeout is based on measured network timing.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which service commonly uses TCP port 22?
questions.explanation: SSH commonly listens on TCP 22 for encrypted remote access.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which service commonly uses TCP port 443?
questions.explanation: HTTPS commonly uses TCP 443; HTTP/3 can instead use QUIC over UDP on that port.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol resolves domain names to records such as IP addresses?
questions.explanation: DNS is a distributed naming system with resource records such as A and AAAA.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: AAAA records contain IPv6 addresses; A records contain IPv4 addresses.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which DNS record type identifies a domain's mail exchanger?
questions.explanation: MX records specify mail servers and their preference values for a domain.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does a DNS record's TTL primarily control?
options: The IP packet's maximum route length
The number of available TCP ports
How long a cached record may be reused
questions.explanation: DNS TTL is a cache lifetime and is distinct from an IP packet's hop-limiting TTL.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which DHCPv4 exchange normally obtains a new lease?
questions.explanation: DORA is the standard initial DHCPv4 lease exchange.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol synchronizes clocks over a network?
questions.explanation: Network Time Protocol synchronizes system time, important for logs and authentication.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol is normally used to send email between mail servers?
questions.explanation: SMTP transfers mail; IMAP and POP3 are primarily for accessing stored mail.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol allows a mail client to synchronize server-side folders?
questions.explanation: IMAP keeps mailbox state and folders on the server and supports synchronization by multiple clients.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol provides network-device monitoring through a management information base?
questions.explanation: SNMP exposes managed objects described by a MIB; secure deployments prefer SNMPv3 with appropriate settings.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is a key security advantage of SNMPv3 over older community-based versions?
options: Support for authentication and privacy protection
questions.explanation: SNMPv3 supports authenticated and encrypted management exchanges when the relevant security level is configured.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which protocol does ping normally use?
questions.explanation: Ping sends ICMP echo requests and receives echo replies; filtering may prevent replies even when a host is reachable.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How does classic traceroute discover successive routers?
options: By sending probes with increasing TTL values
By enumerating every Ethernet MAC address
questions.explanation: Increasing TTL values causes successive routers to return time-exceeded messages, revealing hops when responses are permitted.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which file-transfer protocol operates over SSH?
questions.explanation: SSH File Transfer Protocol uses SSH transport, unlike unencrypted FTP and TFTP.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which access method is associated with Wi-Fi?
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi uses collision avoidance because detecting collisions while transmitting wirelessly is impractical.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which authentication mechanism is commonly used in enterprise Wi-Fi through an authentication server?
questions.explanation: Enterprise Wi-Fi commonly uses 802.1X with EAP and an authentication server such as RADIUS.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which legacy wireless security scheme is unsuitable because of fundamental cryptographic weaknesses?
questions.explanation: WEP's design and IV weaknesses make it obsolete and unsafe.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What distinguishes an SSID from a Wi-Fi password?
options: An SSID is a TCP port
An SSID is the private key
An SSID identifies the wireless network
questions.explanation: The SSID is a network identifier; it is not a secret authentication credential.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which CIA-triad property protects data against unauthorized disclosure?
questions.explanation: Confidentiality restricts disclosure; integrity concerns unauthorized changes and availability concerns usable access.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which CIA-triad property is most directly affected by a service outage?
questions.explanation: Availability means authorized users can access services when needed.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A bank requires a maker and a separate checker for sensitive transfers. Which principle is applied?
questions.explanation: Separating initiation and approval reduces fraud and the impact of one compromised operator.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does least privilege require?
options: Grant only permissions necessary for assigned tasks
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the authority available to users, services and applications.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which is a genuine example of two-factor authentication?
options: A PIN plus a security answer
A password plus a hardware security key
questions.explanation: Two factors come from different categories; a password is knowledge and a hardware key is possession.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does authorization determine after identity is established?
options: Which cipher has the largest block
Which actions the identity may perform
Whether a packet has a checksum
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permissions.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which approach best describes zero trust?
options: Use passwords only at the perimeter
Continuously verify access using identity and context rather than implicit network trust
Trust every device inside the office
questions.explanation: Zero trust avoids assuming that a network location alone makes a user or device trustworthy.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why should a bank collect centralized, time-synchronized security logs?
options: To correlate events and reconstruct incident timelines
questions.explanation: Reliable timestamps and centralized records support detection, correlation and investigation.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which algorithm is symmetric encryption?
questions.explanation: AES uses a shared secret key for encryption and decryption. SHA-256 is a hash, not encryption.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which operation is a cryptographic hash designed to provide?
options: Reversible compression with a secret key
A fixed-length digest of variable-length input
Guaranteed unique output for every possible input
questions.explanation: A hash maps arbitrary-length data to a fixed-size digest; collisions exist mathematically but should be hard to find.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does a digital signature primarily provide when correctly verified with a trusted public key?
questions.explanation: A signature binds data to the signing key and detects changes; it does not hide the message.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why are unique random salts used with password hashes?
options: To hide the algorithm from users
To make identical passwords produce different stored hashes and hinder precomputation
questions.explanation: Salts defeat reusable precomputed tables and identical-hash comparisons; a suitable slow password KDF is still needed.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which is most appropriate for storing user passwords?
options: A salted adaptive password KDF such as Argon2id
questions.explanation: Password KDFs deliberately impose work and may use memory to increase the cost of guessing.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does a TLS server certificate help a client verify?
options: That every stored file is encrypted
That the server will remain available
That the server contains no software bugs
That DNS can never be poisoned
The server's identity through a trusted certificate chain and hostname check
questions.explanation: Certificate validation binds a public key to an identity subject to trust, validity and hostname checks.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which mechanism establishes a shared secret over an insecure channel without directly sending that secret?
questions.explanation: Diffie-Hellman derives a shared secret; authentication is also needed to resist an active man-in-the-middle.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does HMAC use in addition to a hash function?
questions.explanation: HMAC authenticates message integrity using a secret key shared by the communicating parties.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which property is provided by ephemeral key exchange when implemented correctly?
questions.explanation: Forward secrecy limits exposure of past sessions if a long-term authentication key is later compromised.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Is Base64 encoding a confidentiality control?
options: No; it is reversible encoding without a secret
Yes; it requires a private key
Yes; it is equivalent to AES
questions.explanation: Base64 represents bytes as text and can be decoded without any secret.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An email impersonates a bank and directs staff to a fake login page. What is this?
questions.explanation: Phishing uses deceptive messages or sites to trick users into revealing information or performing unsafe actions.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A targeted fraudulent message is tailored to a specific finance employee. What is this commonly called?
questions.explanation: Spear phishing targets particular individuals or organizations using personalized context.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Malware encrypts files and demands payment for restoration. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: Ransomware denies access, often through encryption, and attempts extortion.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An attacker floods a service from many compromised devices. What is this?
questions.explanation: A DDoS attack uses multiple sources to overwhelm a target's resources or connectivity.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the main goal of ARP spoofing on a local network?
options: Associate an attacker's MAC address with another host's IP address
questions.explanation: Forged ARP mappings can redirect local traffic through an attacker or disrupt connectivity.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What distinguishes a worm from a typical file-infecting virus?
options: A virus is a cryptographic hash
A worm can propagate independently across systems
A virus always requires hardware access
questions.explanation: Worms can self-propagate, whereas viruses commonly attach to host files or programs.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A malicious tool records a user's keystrokes. Which term applies?
questions.explanation: A keylogger captures input and may steal credentials or other sensitive information.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is a zero-day vulnerability in common security usage?
options: A flaw for which defenders lack an available fix when it is exposed or exploited
A password that expires at midnight
questions.explanation: Zero-day describes a newly exposed or exploited flaw without an available vendor fix at that point.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which control most directly prevents SQL injection in application queries?
questions.explanation: Binding values separates data from SQL syntax; identifiers still require controlled handling.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which control most directly reduces reflected XSS when showing untrusted text in HTML?
questions.explanation: Output encoding prevents untrusted input from being interpreted as executable markup in the output context.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A browser sends an unwanted authenticated state-changing request from a malicious site. Which threat is this?
questions.explanation: Cross-site request forgery abuses ambient browser credentials; anti-CSRF tokens and suitable cookie settings help mitigate it.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which cookie attribute prevents ordinary JavaScript from reading the cookie?
questions.explanation: HttpOnly restricts script access. Secure controls transmission over secure connections, not script readability.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which cookie attribute restricts sending a cookie to secure connections?
questions.explanation: The Secure attribute limits transmission to secure contexts such as HTTPS; it does not by itself stop script access.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An application accepts a user-controlled URL and fetches an internal metadata endpoint. Which issue is this?
questions.explanation: SSRF causes the server to make attacker-influenced requests, potentially reaching internal resources.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A user changes an account ID in a URL and sees another customer's statement. What control was likely missing?
questions.explanation: Every object access must be authorized for the current user; hiding or randomizing identifiers alone is insufficient.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why should session identifiers be regenerated after login?
questions.explanation: Regeneration prevents an attacker-chosen pre-login session ID from remaining valid after authentication.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is a primary purpose of a firewall?
questions.explanation: A firewall permits or denies traffic according to policy; it is one layer of protection.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How does a stateful firewall differ from a stateless packet filter?
options: It tracks connection state when evaluating traffic
It operates only on paper logs
questions.explanation: Stateful inspection uses context from tracked flows rather than considering only individual packets in isolation.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which control is specifically designed to inspect HTTP application traffic for common web attacks?
questions.explanation: A WAF applies application-aware rules to web traffic; secure application coding remains necessary.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the typical distinction between IDS and IPS?
options: An IDS detects and alerts; an inline IPS can block traffic
An IDS replaces DNS; an IPS replaces DHCP
An IDS always encrypts; an IPS always decrypts
An IDS stores backups; an IPS restores them
Both are identical to unmanaged switches
questions.explanation: Intrusion detection alerts on suspicious activity; intrusion prevention can actively block detected traffic.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why place a public web server in a DMZ?
options: To isolate exposed services from sensitive internal networks
To guarantee the server cannot be attacked
questions.explanation: A DMZ creates a controlled network segment between external exposure and internal systems.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which control best limits lateral movement after a workstation compromise?
options: Network segmentation with restrictive access rules
questions.explanation: Segmentation restricts access between zones, reducing the paths available to an attacker.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What should be done first when an endpoint is actively spreading ransomware, under an established response plan?
options: Contain its network access to limit spread
questions.explanation: Containment limits further damage; investigation and evidence preservation follow the organization's incident response process.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why test backup restoration rather than merely check that backup jobs completed?
options: To avoid keeping any backup copies
To guarantee that no user makes errors
To verify data is recoverable within required objectives
questions.explanation: A successful backup job does not establish that restoration works or meets recovery targets.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does RPO measure?
options: The time to issue a certificate
questions.explanation: Recovery Point Objective concerns acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO concerns restoration time.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does RTO measure?
options: The length of an encryption key
The target maximum time to restore a service
The age of a password hash
questions.explanation: Recovery Time Objective defines the targeted restoration time after disruption.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which backup property is particularly useful against ransomware that tries to alter backup copies?
options: Storing every copy on the same writable share
questions.explanation: Immutable or offline copies reduce the ability of compromised production systems to destroy backups.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is a SIEM system primarily used for?
questions.explanation: Security Information and Event Management aggregates events and supports detection and investigation.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which activity should occur before applying a critical patch to a bank's production server when time permits?
options: Test compatibility and prepare a rollback plan
questions.explanation: Testing and rollback preparation reduce operational risk while addressing the vulnerability promptly.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which security measure is best for an administrator needing temporary elevated access?
options: Time-limited privileged access with audit logging
questions.explanation: Just-in-time privilege reduces standing access and audit logs provide accountability.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does a vulnerability scanner usually identify?
options: The legal owner of each packet
Proof that every finding is exploitable in context
questions.explanation: Scanning finds candidate issues; validation and prioritization are still required.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which error-detection technique uses polynomial division?
questions.explanation: Cyclic redundancy checks treat bit strings as polynomials over a binary field and compute a remainder.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What can a single parity bit reliably detect?
options: Any odd number of bit errors
All burst errors regardless of length
Every possible even number of bit errors
questions.explanation: An odd number of flipped bits changes parity; an even number can leave it unchanged.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which transmission medium is resistant to electromagnetic interference?
questions.explanation: Optical fiber carries light rather than electrical signals and is resistant to electromagnetic interference.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which switching method reserves resources along a path for the duration of a session?
questions.explanation: Circuit switching establishes a dedicated logical circuit, unlike independent datagram forwarding.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which delay is determined primarily by packet length divided by link bit rate?
questions.explanation: Transmission delay is the time to put the packet's bits onto the link: L/R.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which delay depends mainly on physical distance and signal speed in the medium?
questions.explanation: Propagation delay is distance divided by signal propagation speed.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does MTU describe?
options: The largest packet size supported by a link without fragmentation at that layer
The maximum number of users in a domain
The length of a DNS zone name
The size of every TCP window
questions.explanation: A link's MTU limits the packet size it can carry without fragmentation or segmentation at the relevant layer.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which IPv4 header field identifies the encapsulated upper-layer protocol?
questions.explanation: The Protocol field identifies upper-layer payloads, such as TCP value 6 and UDP value 17.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Who performs IPv6 fragmentation when required?
questions.explanation: IPv6 routers do not fragment packets; the source handles fragmentation using path MTU information.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is a default route used for?
options: Only packets addressed to the router itself
Destinations with no more-specific matching route
questions.explanation: A default route is the least-specific match, commonly 0.0.0.0/0 for IPv4.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does an HTTP 503 response commonly indicate?
options: The TLS certificate is valid forever
questions.explanation: 503 Service Unavailable commonly signals overload or maintenance, rather than a successful response.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What does an HTTP 401 response indicate?
options: The server permanently redirected the resource
The request lacks valid authentication credentials
questions.explanation: 401 relates to authentication; 403 generally indicates that access is forbidden.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which deployment best supports high availability during a single server failure?
options: One server with two desktop wallpapers
A single copy of data on one disk
questions.explanation: Redundancy and tested failover allow another instance to serve requests when one fails.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why is certificate hostname validation necessary in TLS?
options: To ensure the certificate identifies the intended server name
questions.explanation: A trusted certificate for a different name must not authenticate the intended server.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which attack tries many common passwords against a small number of accounts?
options: Password spraying across many users with one common password
questions.explanation: Brute forcing tests many guesses for a target; password spraying instead spreads a small set of passwords across many accounts.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which attack reuses leaked username-password pairs against another service?
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing exploits password reuse across services, making unique passwords and MFA valuable.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the purpose of data masking in a non-production bank test environment?
options: Increase the number of public database ports
Reduce exposure of sensitive customer values
Replace referential integrity with plaintext secrets
questions.explanation: Masking substitutes or obscures sensitive values while retaining suitable test characteristics.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which DNS record creates an alias to another canonical hostname?
questions.explanation: A CNAME points a name to another canonical domain name rather than directly storing an IP address.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which DNS record is commonly used for reverse address-to-name lookup?
questions.explanation: Reverse DNS zones use PTR records to associate an address-derived name with a hostname.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is a TCP SYN flood intended to exhaust?
questions.explanation: Many incomplete handshakes can consume connection state; SYN cookies are one mitigation.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A former employee's account is still active. Which process should have removed this access?
questions.explanation: Offboarding should revoke accounts, sessions and access rights promptly.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which control best protects a private signing key used for high-value banking operations?
options: An email attachment to all staff
A suitably managed hardware security module
questions.explanation: An HSM protects key material and can perform cryptographic operations without exposing the private key to ordinary application memory.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Why is encryption at rest insufficient by itself to stop an authorized but compromised application from leaking records?
options: The application may legitimately decrypt data and misuse its access
Encryption at rest always disables authentication
questions.explanation: Encryption protects certain storage threats; application authorization, monitoring and least privilege are still necessary.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a tuple in the relational model?
questions.explanation: A tuple is a row representing one combination of attribute values in a relation.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the degree of a relation?
questions.explanation: Degree counts attributes or columns; cardinality counts tuples or rows.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple?
questions.explanation: A candidate key uniquely identifies tuples and has no unnecessary attribute.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: How does a superkey differ from a candidate key?
options: A candidate key must be nullable
A superkey must be a foreign key
A superkey may contain unnecessary attributes
A candidate key is never unique
questions.explanation: Every candidate key is a minimal superkey; a superkey need not be minimal.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does a foreign key primarily enforce?
options: A fixed number of table rows
questions.explanation: A foreign key requires referencing values to match an allowed referenced key, subject to nullability and constraint rules.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A table has several candidate keys. What is an alternate key?
options: A candidate key not chosen as the primary key
questions.explanation: Candidate keys other than the chosen primary key are called alternate keys.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which constraint directly prevents a required column from containing NULL?
questions.explanation: NOT NULL disallows missing values; a default only supplies a value when its use is triggered.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A balance must never be negative. Which schema feature most directly expresses this row-level rule?
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint validates the predicate for inserted or updated rows; use NOT NULL separately if missing balances are forbidden.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is logical data independence?
options: Changing the logical schema without requiring changes to external views where mappings can preserve them
Changing hardware without any physical schema
questions.explanation: Logical data independence separates external user views from changes in the conceptual schema.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is physical data independence?
options: Changing business meaning without updating applications
Changing storage structures without changing the logical schema
questions.explanation: Storage layout and access methods can change while the logical database interface remains stable.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ER relationship describes one branch having many accounts, each belonging to one branch?
questions.explanation: One branch can relate to multiple accounts while each account relates to one branch.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: How is a many-to-many relationship typically represented in relational tables?
options: With a comma-separated list in every row
With a junction table containing foreign keys to both entities
With a table having no columns
questions.explanation: A junction table represents each association as a row and can store relationship attributes.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What characterizes a weak entity in ER modelling?
options: It always has exactly one row
It has no attributes of any kind
It is stored only in RAM
Its identification depends on an owner entity
questions.explanation: A weak entity uses an owner key together with a partial key for identification.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which is an example of a derived attribute?
options: Age computed from date of birth
A stored date of birth itself
questions.explanation: Age can be calculated from date of birth and a reference date, so it need not be stored independently.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the main objective of normalization?
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes dependencies to reduce redundant facts and insertion, update and deletion anomalies.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does first normal form require in the usual relational teaching model?
options: Atomic attribute values with no repeating groups
questions.explanation: 1NF disallows repeating groups and requires values treated as atomic in their domains.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which dependency is removed when moving from 1NF to 2NF?
options: Every transitive dependency including key attributes
A non-prime attribute's partial dependency on a candidate key
questions.explanation: 2NF requires non-prime attributes to depend on the whole of every candidate key, not a proper subset.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: For a relation to be in BCNF, what must hold for every nontrivial functional dependency X → Y?
options: Y is always a foreign key
questions.explanation: BCNF requires each nontrivial determinant to be a superkey.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: How can 3NF allow a dependency that BCNF disallows?
options: The dependent attribute may be prime even when the determinant is not a superkey
questions.explanation: For a nontrivial X → A, 3NF permits either a superkey determinant or a prime dependent attribute.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a lossless decomposition?
options: Joining decomposed relations reconstructs exactly the original relation
The join always adds extra tuples
questions.explanation: Lossless decomposition avoids both losing original information and introducing spurious tuples on reconstruction.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does dependency preservation allow?
options: Checking original dependencies on the decomposed relations without joining them
Replacing all primary keys with NULL
questions.explanation: Dependency preservation lets constraints be enforced locally on component relations.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: R(A,B,C) has A → B and B → C, with A the only candidate key. What violates 3NF?
options: The lack of a multivalued field
A → B because A is a key
B → C because B is not a superkey and C is non-prime
questions.explanation: The transitive dependency through B violates 3NF because B is not a superkey and C is not prime.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which normal form addresses nontrivial multivalued dependencies whose determinants are not superkeys?
questions.explanation: 4NF strengthens the treatment of independent multivalued facts.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: R(A,B,C) has A → B and B → C. What is A+?
questions.explanation: Start with A, add B using A → B, then add C using B → C.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which SQL clause filters rows before grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual input rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which SQL clause filters aggregated groups?
questions.explanation: HAVING applies conditions to groups and can use aggregate expressions.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which expression counts all rows, including rows whose balance is NULL?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values of that expression.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: How is SQL NULL normally tested?
questions.explanation: NULL comparisons with ordinary equality yield UNKNOWN; IS NULL tests nullness explicitly.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the result of the SQL predicate NULL = NULL in three-valued logic?
options: A syntax error in standard SQL
questions.explanation: NULL represents missing or unknown information, so equality does not establish a true comparison.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which rows pass a SQL WHERE condition?
options: All rows with NULL in any field
Only rows for which the condition is TRUE
questions.explanation: WHERE retains TRUE; FALSE and UNKNOWN are both filtered out.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a SELECT result?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT deduplicates result rows; SELECT ALL retains duplicates.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION removes duplicates while UNION ALL retains them
questions.explanation: UNION performs duplicate elimination; UNION ALL simply combines compatible result rows.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Without ORDER BY, what can a query consumer assume about result order?
questions.explanation: SQL does not guarantee a result order unless ORDER BY specifies it.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which aggregate ignores NULL values when averaging a column?
questions.explanation: AVG averages the non-NULL input values rather than treating NULL as zero.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does COALESCE(a,b,c) return?
questions.explanation: COALESCE evaluates alternatives in order and returns the first non-NULL value.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does DELETE FROM accounts WHERE status='closed' do?
options: Deletes matching rows while retaining the table
questions.explanation: DELETE removes selected rows; DROP TABLE removes the table object.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which command changes an existing table's definition?
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE modifies schema elements; UPDATE modifies row values.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which SQL command grants a privilege to a role?
questions.explanation: GRANT assigns privileges; REVOKE removes them.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Every left row regardless of matches
Only row combinations satisfying the join condition
The Cartesian product regardless of ON
Every right row regardless of matches
questions.explanation: An inner join retains combinations for which the join predicate is true.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does a LEFT JOIN preserve?
options: All rows from both sides in every case
Every left-side row, using NULLs for unmatched right-side columns
questions.explanation: A left outer join keeps left rows even without a match; multiple matches can produce multiple output rows.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: If A has 4 rows and B has 7 rows, how many rows does A CROSS JOIN B produce?
questions.explanation: A Cartesian product pairs each of the four A rows with all seven B rows: 4 × 7 = 28.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Why can filtering a right-table column in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN remove unmatched left rows?
options: The filter can evaluate to UNKNOWN for the NULL-extended rows
LEFT JOIN always removes all left rows
questions.explanation: An unmatched row has NULL right-side values, so many ordinary WHERE comparisons reject it.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which SQL construct checks whether a subquery returns at least one row?
questions.explanation: EXISTS returns true if the subquery has a row; its selected values are generally irrelevant.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Why can NOT IN behave unexpectedly if its subquery includes NULL?
options: The comparison can become UNKNOWN and exclude rows
NULL is always replaced by zero
NULL forces every row to be included
questions.explanation: Three-valued logic means a NULL in the set can prevent a nonmatching value from satisfying NOT IN.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
options: A subquery referring to columns from an outer query
A query that cannot use WHERE
A query that creates a table
A subquery with no FROM clause only
A query that always returns one row
questions.explanation: Correlation links the subquery's evaluation to values from the outer query context.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC, id) assign?
options: A distinct sequential number to each row in that order
The same number to all tied scores
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER generates unique sequence positions; the extra id orders score ties deterministically.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: How does RANK differ from DENSE_RANK for tied values?
options: DENSE_RANK leaves gaps; RANK does not
RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not
questions.explanation: For values 90,90,80, RANK gives 1,1,3 while DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property makes a transaction all-or-nothing?
questions.explanation: Atomicity ensures that partial transaction effects are not retained when the transaction fails.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property preserves committed changes after a crash, subject to the system's guarantees?
questions.explanation: Durability requires committed effects to survive covered failures using durable storage and recovery mechanisms.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property concerns concurrent transactions behaving according to the chosen isolation guarantees?
questions.explanation: Isolation controls interference between concurrent transactions; different isolation levels allow different anomalies.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A transfer debits one account but a failure occurs before the credit. Which property should prevent retaining the partial transfer?
questions.explanation: Both transfer steps must commit together or be rolled back together.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a dirty read?
options: Reading the same committed row twice
questions.explanation: A dirty read can expose values that are later rolled back.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a non-repeatable read?
options: A row is locked before the first read
A transaction writes to its own row twice
A query returns identical values twice
The same row yields a changed committed value when reread in one transaction
An index is read from memory
questions.explanation: A concurrent committed update changes the row between two reads by another transaction.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a phantom anomaly?
options: A row contains an empty string
A query has no ORDER BY
Repeating a predicate query sees newly qualifying or missing rows due to concurrent changes
questions.explanation: Phantoms affect the set of rows satisfying a predicate, often through concurrent insertions or deletions.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which isolation level is intended to make transactions behave as if executed in some serial order?
questions.explanation: Serializable provides the strongest standard isolation semantics, though implementations may use different mechanisms.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a lost update?
options: One concurrent update overwrites another update without preserving its effect
questions.explanation: Read-modify-write sequences can lose changes when concurrent writers operate on stale values without coordination.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does COMMIT do?
options: Successfully ends a transaction and makes its changes committed
Undoes every transaction in the database
questions.explanation: COMMIT marks successful completion; durability then depends on the database's configured guarantees.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the purpose of a SAVEPOINT?
options: Allow rollback to a named point within a transaction
questions.explanation: A savepoint enables partial rollback within an active transaction, subject to database support.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What are the two phases of basic two-phase locking?
options: Growing lock acquisition followed by shrinking lock release
Read phase followed by disk-format phase
questions.explanation: After a transaction releases a lock in the shrinking phase, it cannot acquire new locks under basic 2PL.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What extra restriction does strict two-phase locking commonly impose?
options: All locks are released before writes
Every row uses a different database
Exclusive locks are held until commit or abort
No transaction can read any row
questions.explanation: Holding write locks to transaction end prevents other transactions from reading or overwriting uncommitted writes.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: When can two transactions simultaneously hold shared locks on the same row in a conventional lock manager?
options: Only if both are writing the row
Only if the row has no key
Only after the row is deleted
When neither requests an incompatible exclusive lock
questions.explanation: Shared locks are mutually compatible for readers; an exclusive lock conflicts with them.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does a cycle in a wait-for graph indicate in a single-instance lock setting?
questions.explanation: A directed cycle means each transaction in the cycle waits for a resource held by another.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is MVCC designed to support?
options: Storing every table as a CSV
Concurrent access using multiple versions of data
questions.explanation: Multi-Version Concurrency Control lets readers access suitable versions while writers create newer versions.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is write skew under snapshot isolation?
options: Concurrent transactions update different rows based on a shared old snapshot and jointly violate an invariant
Every transaction writes the same row and always blocks
questions.explanation: Snapshot isolation can avoid some anomalies yet allow write skew where conflicting business logic spans different rows.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a common benefit of an index?
questions.explanation: Indexes speed suitable reads but consume storage and impose maintenance costs on writes.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Why is a B+ tree well suited to range queries?
options: Its ordered leaf entries can be scanned in sequence
questions.explanation: B+ tree leaves preserve key order and are commonly linked for efficient range traversal.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a hash index particularly suited to?
questions.explanation: Hashing distributes keys by hash value and favors equality lookups rather than ordered ranges.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a covering index for a query?
options: A backup of the entire server
A view that cannot be read
An index containing all columns needed to answer that query
An index on every database automatically
An index with no leaf pages
questions.explanation: If needed values are available in the index, the engine may avoid separate table-row access.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: For a conventional B-tree index on (branch_id, customer_id), which predicate most directly uses the leading-column order?
options: status IS NULL with no indexed column
questions.explanation: The leading branch_id constrains a contiguous index range; optimization of non-leading columns varies by engine.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Why can too many indexes slow down INSERT operations?
options: Each affected index must also be maintained
An insert must always scan every table
questions.explanation: Writing a row entails changes to relevant indexes in addition to table storage and logging.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does a query execution plan describe?
options: The password of the database owner
The operations and access paths chosen to execute a query
questions.explanation: Execution plans expose scans, joins, sorts and other operators used to evaluate a query.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A predicate selects a very small fraction of rows. How is its selectivity commonly described?
questions.explanation: A highly selective predicate narrows the result substantially and can benefit from an appropriate index.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the key rule of write-ahead logging?
options: Logs are stored only after a crash
Data pages must always be written before logs
Log information must reach durable storage before corresponding dirty data pages are written
questions.explanation: WAL ensures recovery information is durable before data-page changes dependent on it reach storage.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a database checkpoint primarily used to reduce?
options: The recovery work needed after a crash
questions.explanation: Checkpoints record recovery progress and limit how far recovery must process earlier activity.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which backup contains changes since the last full backup?
options: Incremental backup since the last backup of any type
questions.explanation: A differential backup accumulates changes since the last full backup; an incremental commonly captures changes since the last backup.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is required for point-in-time recovery in a typical log-based database?
options: A suitable base backup and the needed transaction-log sequence
Only the latest screenshot of a table
questions.explanation: Restoring a base backup and replaying logs to a target time recovers an intermediate state when supported.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Why is replication not a complete substitute for backups?
options: Accidental deletions or corruption may replicate to replicas
Backups are always faster than replication
questions.explanation: Replication improves availability but can copy undesirable changes; independent retained backups support recovery.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is an ordinary SQL view?
options: A named query presenting a virtual table
Always a separate stored copy of every result row
questions.explanation: An ordinary view stores a query definition; a materialized view stores results and has refresh considerations.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What distinguishes a materialized view from an ordinary view?
options: It stores query results that may need refreshing
It is always identical to a foreign key
questions.explanation: Stored results can speed reads but must be refreshed according to the system's freshness requirements.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a trigger?
options: Code automatically invoked by specified database events
questions.explanation: Triggers execute in response to configured events such as inserts or updates; details depend on the DBMS.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a cursor commonly used for?
options: Processing a query result incrementally, often row by row
questions.explanation: A cursor provides controlled traversal of a result set; set-based SQL is often preferable where suitable.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which workload best describes OLTP?
questions.explanation: OLTP supports day-to-day transactions such as deposits, withdrawals and transfers.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which workload best describes OLAP?
options: Analytical queries over large historical datasets
questions.explanation: OLAP supports multidimensional analysis, reporting and aggregations.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: In a star schema, what does the central fact table usually contain?
options: Measures and foreign keys to dimensions
Every dimension's entire text hierarchy only
questions.explanation: Fact tables record measures such as amounts and reference dimensions such as date, branch and product.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does ETL stand for?
questions.explanation: ETL obtains source data, transforms it and loads it into a target such as a warehouse.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does sharding typically do?
options: Duplicates every row on every node only
Stores all data in one CPU register
questions.explanation: Sharding distributes subsets of rows, commonly by a shard key, across nodes.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: In the CAP discussion, what is the trade-off during a network partition?
options: A system cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability for every request
Durability is impossible even on one node
A database can never store rows
All SQL constraints must be removed
questions.explanation: CAP concerns the limits of simultaneously guaranteeing consistency and availability when communication is partitioned.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is eventual consistency?
options: Every read always sees the latest global write
Replicas converge if updates stop and communication succeeds
All replicas must be identical at every instant
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency allows temporary divergence but expects convergence under the required conditions.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the role of the prepare phase in two-phase commit?
options: Create an index on every column
Ask participants whether they can commit the distributed transaction
questions.explanation: Participants prepare and vote; the coordinator then decides commit or abort in the second phase.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which permission is most suitable for a reporting account that only needs to read approved views?
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the read access needed, preferably through controlled views when appropriate.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which control helps prevent accidental duplicate payment processing when a request is retried?
options: A unique idempotency key recorded transactionally
questions.explanation: A unique request identifier checked within the transaction lets the application recognize and safely handle retries.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which storage type is generally more appropriate than binary floating point for exact monetary amounts?
options: A binary floating-point type without rounding policy
questions.explanation: Fixed-precision decimal represents decimal amounts exactly within its defined precision and scale; applications still need explicit rounding rules.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which SQL expression returns 0 when balance is NULL and otherwise returns balance?
questions.explanation: COALESCE chooses balance if non-NULL, otherwise zero. NULLIF has a different purpose.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does NULLIF(a,b) return when a equals b?
questions.explanation: NULLIF returns NULL when its two arguments compare equal, otherwise the first argument.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: R(A,B,C) has AB → C and A → B. What is a candidate key?
options: AC only, with A not a key
questions.explanation: A determines B and therefore AB; AB determines C, so A determines all attributes and is minimal.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does optimistic concurrency control typically check before committing?
options: Whether concurrent changes invalidate the transaction's assumptions
Whether the database name is uppercase
Whether every table has one row
questions.explanation: Optimistic methods validate at commit or update time, often using version values, and retry or reject conflicting work.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Why can wrapping an indexed column in a function make a simple index less useful?
options: The predicate may no longer match the index's stored ordering or expression
Every function automatically corrupts the table
The query must become a cross join
questions.explanation: A plain column index may not support the expression efficiently; an appropriate expression index or rewritten predicate can help.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does PARTITION BY branch_id do inside a window function?
options: Restarts the window calculation separately for each branch
Groups rows into one output row per branch automatically
questions.explanation: Window partitioning defines independent groups for calculation while preserving individual result rows.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What distinguishes an incremental backup in the usual backup-chain model?
options: It can never depend on an earlier backup
It always captures every database page
It captures changes since the most recent backup in the chain
questions.explanation: Incremental restoration commonly requires the base full backup and subsequent increments in order.

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property requires a transaction to preserve declared database rules when starting from a valid state?
questions.explanation: ACID consistency concerns valid state transitions under constraints; application logic must also correctly enforce its business rules.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a process?
options: A program in execution with its execution state and resources
questions.explanation: A process includes an executing program, address space, registers and managed resources.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which data structure records a process's state, registers and scheduling information?
questions.explanation: The PCB holds information the OS needs to manage and resume a process.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is saved and restored during a context switch?
options: Only the file names on disk
Execution context such as CPU registers and program counter
questions.explanation: The OS saves the outgoing execution state and restores the incoming one; switching has overhead.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which state normally describes a process waiting for disk I/O to complete?
questions.explanation: A blocked process cannot proceed until the awaited event occurs; a ready process can run once scheduled.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What do threads in the same process normally share?
options: Separate unrelated virtual address spaces always
Address space and open process resources
questions.explanation: Threads share process memory/resources but have their own registers, program counter and stacks.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a zombie process on Unix-like systems?
options: A terminated child whose exit status has not yet been collected
A process currently using all CPU cores
A process that never had a parent
questions.explanation: The child has exited, but a process-table entry remains until the parent reaps its status.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does fork() normally do on Unix-like systems?
options: Replace the current program image only
Wait for a child to terminate
questions.explanation: fork creates a child, commonly using copy-on-write address-space duplication.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does a successful exec-family call do?
options: Replace the current process image with a new program
questions.explanation: exec loads a new program into the current process and does not return on success.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which scheduling method gives each ready process a time quantum in cyclic order?
questions.explanation: Round robin rotates ready tasks, using preemption at quantum boundaries.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a disadvantage of choosing an extremely small round-robin quantum?
questions.explanation: Frequent timer-driven switches spend more time on scheduling overhead rather than useful work.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which algorithm minimizes average waiting time for a set of available jobs when burst lengths are known and overhead is ignored?
options: First come first served in arbitrary order
questions.explanation: Serving shorter jobs first minimizes average waiting time under the stated assumptions.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is starvation?
options: A task waits indefinitely because others repeatedly get preferred service
questions.explanation: Starvation can occur under unfair scheduling or resource allocation even without deadlock.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which technique mitigates starvation in priority scheduling?
options: Giving new tasks permanent maximum priority
questions.explanation: Aging gradually raises the priority of tasks that have waited too long.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is turnaround time?
options: First CPU start minus arrival only
CPU burst divided by queue length
Time spent only in kernel mode
questions.explanation: Turnaround includes the total elapsed time from arrival to completion.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is response time in interactive scheduling?
options: Time from arrival until the task first receives CPU service
questions.explanation: Response time measures the initial wait before first service, distinct from total turnaround.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a race condition?
options: An application uses only one immutable variable
An outcome depends on uncontrolled interleaving of concurrent accesses
questions.explanation: Unsynchronized access to shared state can make results depend on timing.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a critical section?
options: Code accessing shared state that requires controlled concurrent access
questions.explanation: Synchronization protects operations that must not interleave unsafely.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is the main purpose of a mutex?
options: Provide mutual exclusion for a critical section
Schedule every process by shortest job
questions.explanation: A mutex allows one owner at a time to enter the protected section.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: How can a counting semaphore be used?
options: Limit concurrent access to a pool of a fixed number of resources
questions.explanation: A semaphore count represents available permits; wait acquires and signal releases a permit.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is busy waiting?
options: Repeatedly checking a condition while consuming CPU
Sleeping until an interrupt without consuming CPU
questions.explanation: Spin-waiting checks repeatedly and can waste CPU when waits are long.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Why should a condition-variable wait generally recheck its predicate in a loop?
options: A wakeup always means the thread must terminate
The predicate may be false after wakeup, including spurious wakeups or another thread's action
The mutex must never be reacquired
questions.explanation: Wakeup is a reason to recheck the condition under the lock, not proof that it still holds.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which is one of the Coffman conditions for deadlock?
questions.explanation: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait in the classical model.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Imposing a global order on lock acquisition primarily prevents which deadlock condition?
questions.explanation: If all tasks acquire locks in one consistent order, cyclic lock dependencies cannot form.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does Banker's algorithm test before granting a request?
options: Whether the process has the largest PID
Whether the resulting state can remain safe
questions.explanation: The algorithm grants requests only when a safe completion sequence remains possible under declared maximum claims.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Does an unsafe resource-allocation state necessarily mean deadlock has already occurred?
options: No; it means a safe completion sequence is not guaranteed
No; unsafe means all tasks have completed
No; unsafe means all resources are unlimited
Yes; it means no resources exist
Yes; unsafe and deadlocked are identical
questions.explanation: An unsafe state may lead to deadlock depending on future requests; deadlock is an actual inability to proceed.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is virtual memory primarily intended to provide?
options: An address-space abstraction independent of the exact physical-memory layout
One shared password for all processes
questions.explanation: Virtual memory maps process-visible addresses to physical memory and other backing arrangements.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a page fault?
options: An access requires OS handling because the page mapping is absent or violates access conditions
questions.explanation: A not-present page fault may load a page; protection faults may instead cause an error or other OS action.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a TLB?
questions.explanation: The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-to-physical translation information.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What type of fragmentation is associated with unused space inside an allocated fixed-size page frame?
questions.explanation: Fixed-size allocation can leave unused space inside the last allocated unit.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is external fragmentation?
options: Unused bytes within a fixed allocated page only
Free memory exists in separated holes too small for a needed contiguous allocation
questions.explanation: External fragmentation concerns scattered free regions outside allocated blocks.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: How does paging differ from segmentation in its usual model?
options: Paging uses fixed-size units; segmentation uses variable-size logical regions
Segmentation always uses fixed-size pages only
Paging eliminates every form of overhead
Paging requires all programs to be one contiguous block
questions.explanation: Pages are uniform-sized; segments correspond to logical regions with variable lengths.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is demand paging?
options: Writing all pages on every instruction
Loading a page when it is needed rather than loading all pages in advance
questions.explanation: Demand paging brings in pages as references require them.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is thrashing?
options: A page table with one entry
Excessive paging that leaves little useful CPU progress
questions.explanation: When working sets exceed available memory, frequent faults and paging can dominate execution.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which page-replacement policy removes the page not used for the longest time in the past?
questions.explanation: LRU uses past recency, while the optimal policy would need knowledge of future references.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which policy can exhibit Belady's anomaly?
questions.explanation: FIFO can incur more faults with more frames for some reference strings; stack algorithms avoid this anomaly.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which replacement policy gives a theoretical minimum number of faults for a known reference string?
options: Always replace the smallest page number
Always replace the oldest loaded page
Replace the page whose next use is farthest in the future
Never replace any page regardless of capacity
questions.explanation: The optimal policy is a benchmark requiring future knowledge unavailable in ordinary online operation.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is copy-on-write?
options: Copy every page on each read
Share pages until a write requires a private copy
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write defers copying until modification, reducing unnecessary duplication after operations such as fork.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does a process working set represent?
options: Pages actively referenced during a recent execution interval
questions.explanation: Working-set estimates help understand the resident memory needed to avoid excessive paging.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does a Unix inode normally contain?
options: The DNS name of the host
A copy of the entire directory path always
The filename as its sole identifying field
File metadata and references to data blocks
questions.explanation: Directory entries map names to inode numbers; inodes hold metadata and data-location information.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a hard link?
options: A copy of file data on every read
Another directory entry referencing the same inode
questions.explanation: Hard links share the same underlying file object and normally cannot cross filesystem boundaries.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does a symbolic link store?
options: A copy of every target data block
questions.explanation: A symlink references a path and can become dangling if that path no longer resolves.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Why can a deleted file continue using disk space while a process has it open?
options: The disk never reuses any block
The file object remains referenced until the open handle is closed
The inode changes into a network socket
questions.explanation: Unlink removes a name, but storage can remain allocated until all relevant references are gone.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a filesystem journal primarily used for?
options: Help restore structural consistency after interruption
Guarantee every application transaction is atomic
questions.explanation: Journaling records planned changes so recovery can complete or undo incomplete filesystem operations; guarantees vary by mode.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is the main purpose of mounting a filesystem?
options: Attach it to a location in the directory hierarchy
questions.explanation: Mounting makes a filesystem accessible through a mount point.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does RAID 1 primarily provide?
questions.explanation: RAID 1 keeps duplicate copies across disks; it does not replace independent backups.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a key limitation of RAID 0?
options: It always stores two full copies
No redundancy against a member-disk failure
It always uses less than one disk
questions.explanation: RAID 0 stripes data but lacks redundancy; losing a member can lose the array's data.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: How many member-disk failures can conventional RAID 5 tolerate?
questions.explanation: RAID 5 uses distributed single parity and tolerates one member failure; RAID 6 uses double parity.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does the SCAN disk scheduling algorithm do on a rotating disk?
options: Always chooses only the newest request
Moves the head in one direction serving requests, then reverses
questions.explanation: SCAN resembles an elevator, serving requests along its sweep before reversing direction.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Why are seek-optimization algorithms less relevant for SSDs than for rotating disks?
options: SSDs have no latency at all
SSDs have no mechanical seek head
questions.explanation: SSDs still have performance constraints, but mechanical head movement is absent.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is the purpose of user mode and kernel mode separation?
options: Allow any program to overwrite kernel memory
Make every application a kernel module
Restrict privileged operations to controlled OS execution
questions.explanation: Hardware privilege levels protect core resources and mediate access through OS interfaces.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a system call?
options: A controlled request from a program for an OS service
Only a call to another user process
questions.explanation: System calls cross into the kernel to request services such as file I/O or process management.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is an interrupt?
options: A signal causing the CPU to handle an event through an appropriate handler
questions.explanation: Interrupts allow hardware and other events to request attention; precise classifications vary by architecture.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is DMA used for?
options: Transfer data between devices and memory with reduced per-byte CPU intervention
Run all processes in user mode
Encrypt every disk sector by definition
questions.explanation: Direct Memory Access lets hardware perform transfers while the CPU coordinates rather than copying every byte.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which IPC mechanism naturally provides a byte stream between related Unix processes?
questions.explanation: Pipes provide stream communication and are commonly used between commands or related processes.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What additional issue must programs handle when using shared-memory IPC?
options: No process can write shared data
Only one process may map it ever
Mandatory network routing for every byte
Every shared byte must be encrypted by hardware
questions.explanation: Shared memory avoids copying but does not automatically coordinate readers and writers.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a hypervisor?
options: A layer that creates and manages virtual machines
questions.explanation: A hypervisor virtualizes computing resources so guest systems can run in isolated virtual machines.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: How do ordinary OS-level containers differ from separate virtual machines?
options: Containers usually share the host kernel
Every container must boot a separate full guest kernel
